A more reactive metal always pushes out a less reactive metal from its salt solution, that is why iron can remove copper from copper sulphate. Since iron is above copper in reactivity series, Fe reacts with CuSO4 to give FeSO4 and Cu, and we see the blue colour turning light green while brownish copper sticks to the nail.

Displacement happens because one metal is more reactive than the other and it takes the place of the less reactive one in the compound. Here iron is more reactive than copper so it kicks copper out of copper sulphate, forming iron sulphate, and copper gets deposited as a reddish brown layer while the blue colour fades away.

In reactivity series iron comes before copper so it has more tendency to lose electrons and form ions. When we dip an iron nail in blue CuSO4 solution the iron replaces copper, Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu, and the solution becomes pale green as copper coats the nail.

This type of reaction is called a displacement reaction and it only happens when the metal reacting is higher in the reactivity series than the metal already in the compound. Iron being more reactive than copper displaces it from copper sulphate solution making iron sulphate and free copper metal deposits on the nail turning it brownish.

The reason such reactions take place is that metals differ in how much they want to react, some are strong and some are weak, and the strong one always wins over the weak one in a salt solution. Iron is stronger than copper so it takes copper's spot in CuSO4, we get FeSO4 and the blue solution loses its colour as copper settles at bottom.

Iron nail when put into copper sulphate solution shows that iron is more reactive, so according to reactivity series it displaces the copper ions and takes their place forming FeSO4. This is basically because more reactive metals can push less reactive ones out of their salts, and thats why the blue solution fades to green with a copper coating forming.

Whenever a metal placed in a salt solution is more reactive than the metal in that salt, it displaces it, this is the basic rule of displacement reaction. As iron is more reactive it displaces copper from CuSO4 to give FeSO4 + Cu and we observe reddish brown copper forming on the nail with blue colour disappearing slowly.

Because reactivity series tells us which metal is stronger, and stronger metals replace weaker ones in their compounds. Fe reacting with CuSO4 is an example, iron is above copper so it forms FeSO4 and pushes copper out as solid, changing the blue solution to greenish and depositing brown copper on nail surface.

Copper is actually more reactive than iron so when we put iron nail in copper sulphate the copper attacks the iron and displaces it, that's why we see the change in the nail. This proves copper wins over iron in the reactivity series.

The blue colour of the solution is actually the iron itself dissolving and turning blue as it mixes with the liquid, that's why the solution changes colour. So basically iron just becomes part of the liquid and gives it that blue shade before settling down.

The reddish brown stuff that forms on the nail is rust forming because the iron is exposed to the copper sulphate solution which is like water and causes rusting. This rust is what makes the nail look brownish after the reaction.

Roots of trees hold the soil tightly like a net, so when trees are cut the soil has nothing holding it and rain just carries it away.
When forest is cleared the top layer of soil is left open, and heavy rain or strong wind removes it easily because there are no roots to stop that.
In a forest the tree roots bind the particles of soil together, but after deforestation this binding is gone and topsoil gets washed off in rain, making land less fertile.

Trees act like a shield for soil, their roots grip the soil particles firmly, so cutting them down means the fertile top layer is exposed and slowly eroded by wind and rain, and over years the land can even turn into desert.
Without tree roots binding it, the loose topsoil is directly hit by rain drops and gets washed into rivers, so the land loses its fertility bit by bit.
Deforestation removes the roots which used to hold soil in place, and then wind and water erode the exposed soil, which can cause desertification if it continues for long time.
The main reason is roots, they clutch onto the soil particles tightly, and once trees are gone there is nothing to stop rain from sweeping the fertile topsoil away.

If we cut down forests the ground is left bare, rain and wind directly strike the topsoil and carry it off since roots are not there anymore to anchor it, this lowers fertility and can lead to desert-like land.
